lead: Leaching pulls a soluble solute out of a solid with a liquid solvent. The solvent must wet the solid, dissolve the solute, and diffuse back out. The spent solid always leaves wet, carrying solution with it. So the balance is written on the inert solid, which does not dissolve, and on the solution retained per kg of that inert. This is used to extract oil from seeds, sugar from cane, caffeine from coffee, and metals from ores.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the idea of a distribution between two phases, and Unit 2 for equilibrium stages.

sections.h3: The leaching idea and the inert basis

blocks.text: Leaching is solid-liquid extraction. A liquid solvent enters the pores of a solid, dissolves the soluble part, and the solution diffuses back to the bulk liquid. The solid that does not dissolve is the inert or carrier solid. After contact, the mixture is separated into two streams. The overflow is clear solution, rich in solute. The underflow is spent solid plus the solution that stays with it. That retained solution is the main loss of solute; the spent solid is not dry.

Calculations use the inert solid as the fixed basis because its mass does not change. Let I be kg of inert solid in the feed. Let r be kg of solution retained per kg of inert solid in the underflow. Then the underflow carries L = rI kg of solution. Let X be kg of solute per kg of solution. The same X is used for overflow and underflow when the stage is ideal. The ideal stage assumes the solution inside the solid pores and the bulk solution have the same composition after enough contact. Real stages approach this; stage efficiency measures how close they get.

blocks.where: L is kg of solution retained in the underflow; r is kg of solution per kg of inert solid; I is kg of inert solid in the feed.

blocks.text: This basis is used for oilseeds, sugar cane, coffee beans, herbal roots and leached ores. In every case the spent solid leaves wet, so the balance must include that wet solution.

For one equilibrium stage with constant r, write three quantities. Total solution M is all solution after contact: soluble solute in the feed + any liquid already in the feed + the fresh solvent stream. For a dry feed with no liquid, M = m<sub>solute,in</sub> + S. Underflow solution L = rI. Overflow solution V = M − L. At equilibrium both leave at the same X, so X = total solute in solution/M. Solute in overflow = VX. For pure solvent and dry feed, Recovery = VX/(solute originally in solid feed) × 100%. If the solvent is not pure, the equilibrium X includes the solute it brings. Recovery of feed solute is then (VX − solute in fresh solvent)/(solute originally in solid feed) × 100%. This calculation assumes that all soluble solute dissolves and the solution is unsaturated. For a saturated stage, X is the solubility limit and any undissolved solute is balanced separately.

M = m<sub>solute,in</sub> + m<sub>liquid,in</sub> + S;  L = rI;  V = M − L;  X = (m<sub>solute,in</sub> + m<sub>solute,S</sub>)/M;  Recovery = (VX − m<sub>solute,S</sub>)/m<sub>solute,solid</sub> × 100%
blocks.where: M is total kg of solution after contact; m<sub>solute,in</sub> is kg of soluble solute originally in the feed, including any already dissolved in feed liquid; m<sub>solute,solid</sub> is kg of soluble solute originally in the solid feed only (equal to m<sub>solute,in</sub> for dry feed); m<sub>liquid,in</sub> is kg of liquid already in the feed, not counting solute; S is total kg of fresh solvent stream; m<sub>solute,S</sub> is kg of solute in that solvent (0 if pure); L is kg of solution retained in the underflow; r is kg solution per kg inert solid; I is kg inert solid; V is kg of overflow solution; X is kg solute per kg solution at equilibrium, assuming all soluble solute dissolves and the solution is unsaturated. For a saturated stage, X is the solubility limit and undissolved solute is balanced separately. Recovery is % of m<sub>solute,solid</sub> in the overflow.

blocks.text: Cross-current leaching repeats this contact. The underflow from stage 1, still carrying L kg solution at X1, meets W kg fresh solvent in stage 2. For pure solvent and constant L and W, stage 2 gives X2 = X1 L/(L+W). Each stage multiplies the solute fraction by the same factor L/(L+W). Fresh solvent at every stage gives a fast drop in X, but it makes a large volume of dilute overflow. Longer trains are handled in 5.7.

Stage efficiency corrects the ideal stage. X<sub>in</sub> is the composition of the solution entering the stage. X<sub>out</sub> is the actual composition of the solution leaving the stage. X* is the composition that would leave at equilibrium with X<sub>in</sub>. Define E = (X<sub>in</sub> − X<sub>out</sub>)/(X<sub>in</sub> − X*) × 100%. E is below 100% when contact time is short or the solute must diffuse out of thick solids.

Batch agitated vessel. A tank with an agitator contacts solid and solvent. After the set time, the slurry is filtered or centrifuged. It is simple and flexible, used for herbal extraction and small oil batches. The spent cake still holds solution, so washing may be needed.

Pachuca tank. A tall cylindrical tank with an air lift. Compressed air rises in a central pipe and lifts slurry, which circulates down the annulus. There are no moving parts inside, so it handles fine solids and corrosive liquors. It is common in ore leaching.

Dorr agitator and thickener. The Dorr agitator gives continuous mechanical agitation. The Dorr thickener is a shallow settling tank with a rotating rake. Clear overflow leaves at the top; settled underflow is withdrawn at the bottom. A thickener does not dissolve solute; it separates solution from solids.

Continuous counter-current decantation (CCD). Several thickeners are connected in series. Solids move forward from thickener to thickener; wash liquid moves backward. Each thickener is one contact stage. The train recovers solute from the underflow with fresh water or solvent. Named continuous units include the Bollman, Hildebrandt, Crown and Bonotto extractors for oilseeds. Moving beds and percolation are in 5.7.

spec.title: One leaching stage
spec.aria: Solid feed and solvent enter the leacher, and two streams leave: a strong solution overflow and a spent solid underflow still carrying retained solution.

examples.question: 1000 kg of a solid containing 20 mass% oil and 80 mass% inert material is leached in one stage with 500 kg of pure solvent. The spent solid retains 0.5 kg of solution per kg of inert solid. Find the oil recovered in the overflow and the percentage recovery.
steps: Total solution M = oil feed + solvent = 200 + 500 = 700 kg.
Overflow solution V = M − L = 700 − 400 = 300 kg.
At equilibrium X = oil feed / M = 200 / 700 = 0.285714 kg oil/kg solution.
examples.answer: The overflow carries 85.71 kg of oil, a recovery of 42.86%.
examples.check:
inert = 1000 * 0.80
oil_feed = 1000 * 0.20
solvent = 500.0
r = 0.5
L = r * inert
M = oil_feed + solvent
V = M - L
X = oil_feed / M
oil_overflow = V * X
recovery = oil_overflow / oil_feed * 100
print(round(oil_overflow, 2))
print(round(recovery, 2))

traps: Balancing on total solid mass instead of inert mass, so rI is wrong.
Forgetting that the underflow carries solution, then treating the overflow as all the solvent plus all the solute.
Using r as kg solution per kg dry solid including solute, or as kg solvent per kg inert; check the definition.
Assuming overflow mass equals solvent charged; here V = M − rI, not S.

quiz.q: Define r and X in leaching.
quiz.a: r is kg of solution retained per kg of inert solid in the underflow. X is kg of solute per kg of solution.

quiz.q: Why is the balance written on inert solid instead of total solid?
quiz.a: Inert solid mass does not change during leaching. Total solid mass changes because solute leaves the solid, so the inert basis stays fixed and gives a reliable frame for r and L.

quiz.q: A spent solid contains 800 kg inert and retains r = 0.45 kg solution per kg inert. What mass of solution leaves with the spent solid?
One stage has 100 kg solute in feed, 400 kg pure solvent, and rI = 200 kg solution. Find X and the solute in the overflow.
quiz.a: M = 100 + 400 = 500 kg. L = 200 kg. V = 500 − 200 = 300 kg. X = 100/500 = 0.2 kg solute/kg solution. Solute in overflow = 300 × 0.2 = 60 kg.

quiz.q: A student balances total solid mass and predicts no solute in the underflow. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The underflow is not dry solid. It carries L = rI kg of solution at composition X, so solute in underflow is LX. Ignoring that retained solution hides most of the lost solute.

quiz.q: In one stage, adding more solvent raises recovery but makes the overflow weaker. Explain using the formulas.
quiz.a: More solvent raises M and V = M − L. X = solute entering/M falls, but VX can still rise, so recovery rises. The overflow becomes more dilute because X is smaller. The trade-off is more solvent to handle and recover.

quiz.q: What does stage efficiency mean in leaching?
quiz.a: E compares actual and equilibrium change. X<sub>in</sub> is the composition of the solution entering the stage; X<sub>out</sub> is the actual composition of the solution leaving the stage; X* is the composition that would leave at equilibrium with X<sub>in</sub>. E = (X<sub>in</sub> − X<sub>out</sub>)/(X<sub>in</sub> − X*) × 100%.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial CCD trains are common in gold and alumina leaching, sugar diffusion and oilseed extraction. Real retention r changes with solid size, drainage time and solution viscosity, so plants measure a retention curve instead of using one constant. Research looks at solvent choice, ultrasound and pulsed flow to speed up diffusion out of the solid. Search for counter-current decantation, Bollman extractor, solid-liquid extraction and retention curve in leaching.
